docs.title: Out of Tune:  Demystifying Noise-Effects  on Quantum Fourier Models
docs.text:
This is website contains supplementary results to our paper "Out of Tune: Demystifying Noise-Effects on Quantum Fourier Models" available on ArXiv .

Checkout the subpages for detailled plots on how noise affects Coefficients, Training, Entanglement and Expressibility . The Setup page summarises the noise models, ansätze and experimental protocol that all results share. In addition to our Github repository, we provide a reproduction package on Zenodo.

docs.title: Abstract
docs.text:
Variational quantum algorithms have received substantial theoretical and empirical attention. As the underlying variational quantum circuits (VQCs) can be represented by Fourier series whose spectra grow exponentially with the number of input features, hope for quantum advantage remains. Nevertheless, whether and how quantum Fourier models (QFMs) can outperform classical alternatives remains an open question, as the sources of non-classical computational power (for instance, the role of entanglement) are not yet fully understood. Likewise, hardware noise continues to pose a challenge along the path towards fault-tolerant quantum computers.

In this work, we study VQCs through Fourier analysis to better understand their properties and quantify their constraints. We seek to elucidate critical characteristics of QFMs under the influence of noise. Specifically, we undertake a systematic investigation into the impact of noise on the Fourier spectrum, expressibility, and entangling capability of QFMs through extensive numerical simulations and link these properties to training performance. The insights may inform more efficient utilisation of quantum hardware and support the design of tailored error mitigation and correction strategies.

Even without noise, frequency availability does not guarantee a match to the target coefficients within the optimisation budget. Under the tested conditions, decoherent gate errors applied throughout the circuit contract coefficient magnitudes and degrade fitting, while boundary noise and fixed additive coherent errors have smaller effects. Sampled expressibility and entangling capability do not consistently rank fitting performance, while frequency-resolved coefficient errors identify the remaining mismatch with the target.

docs.title: Coefficients
docs.text:
The resulting plots of our experiments as PDF can be found in plotting/rplots/img-gen, while a PNG version can be found on this website.

We characterise the Fourier coefficients of a QFM by sampling the trainable parameters and computing the absolute coefficient mean \(\mu_c(\boldsymbol{\omega})\) and the relative standard deviation \(\sigma_c(\boldsymbol{\omega})\) (normalised by \(\mu_c(\boldsymbol{\omega})\)) for each frequency \(\boldsymbol{\omega}\) via the FFT. All plots show the mean over the seeds, as the standard deviation across seeds is small. In the plots, the ansätze are abbreviated as SEA (Strongly Entangling Ansatz), HEA (Hardware Efficient Ansatz), RYA (RY-Rotation-Only Ansatz) and CRA (Controlled Rotation Ansatz), and the noise types as BF (Bit Flip), PF (Phase Flip), DP (Depolarizing), SP (State Preparation), ME (Measurement), AD (Amplitude Damping), PD (Phase Damping) and CGE (Coherent Gate Error), see Setup.

docs.title: Influence of Input Encoding
docs.text:
We measure the coefficients for \([3\dots 6]\) qubits and \(R_{\{X, Y, Z\}}\) encodings over frequencies in a noiseless setting.

Our Figure 2a from the paper:

Absolute coefficient mean \(\mu_c(\boldsymbol{\omega})\) over frequencies for \([3\dots 6]\) qubits and \(R_{\{X, Y, Z\}}\) encodings in the noiseless setting.

The absolute coefficient mean decreases with the frequency for all ansätze and encodings. Only the SEA and the CRA consistently provide the full spectrum, and only the SEA does so with coefficients that remain of comparable magnitude across frequencies, while the HEA does not reach the highest frequencies for larger qubit counts (an absolute coefficient mean below \(10^{-14}\) is treated as numerically zero).

The corresponding relative standard deviation (Our Figure 11 in the paper, Appendix "Relative Standard Deviation of the Coefficients"):

Relative standard deviation \(\sigma_c(\boldsymbol{\omega})\) of the coefficients for \([3\dots 6]\) qubits and \(R_{\{X, Y, Z\}}\) encodings over frequencies in the noiseless setting, corresponding to the absolute coefficient mean in Fig. 2a.

In contrast to the mean, the relative standard deviation increases with frequency for all encodings and ansätze. Since \(\sigma_c(\boldsymbol{\omega})\) is normalised by the absolute coefficient mean \(\mu_c(\boldsymbol{\omega})\), this does not indicate a larger absolute spread: the absolute standard deviation of the coefficients decreases exponentially with the frequency index, but the mean decays faster, so high-frequency coefficients vary more strongly across parameter samples relative to their magnitude. Furthermore, the relative standard deviation reached at the highest frequency grows with the number of qubits, whereas at a fixed frequency it decreases with the qubit count.

Our Figure 2b from the paper:

Coefficients of six-qubit circuits, separated into real and imaginary parts for different single qubit Pauli-encodings. The individual frequency components are colour-coded.

While there is no obvious difference in \(\mu_c(\boldsymbol{\omega})\) between the encodings, the RYA only exhibits an imaginary part in the coefficients for the \(R_Y\) encoding: with \(R_X\) or \(R_Z\) encoding, all gates, the initial state and the \(Z\) readout are real up to the conjugation symmetry \(R_X(x)^* = R_X(-x)\) and \(R_Z(x)^* = R_Z(-x)\), such that \(f(-x, \boldsymbol{\theta}) = f(x, \boldsymbol{\theta})\) and the coefficients are real. Therefore, the \(R_Y\) encoding is used for the one-dimensional results in the main text of the paper. Apart from this exception, the coefficients are evenly distributed in the real and imaginary part with no clear correlation, which is corroborated by the covariance plots on the coefficients RX, coefficients RY and 2D-coefficients pages.

docs.title: Noise Influence on Spectrum
docs.text:
The absolute coefficient mean and the relative standard deviation under each noise type for six-qubit circuits with \(R_Y\) encoding are shown as Figure 4 and Figure 12 in the paper; both are shown on the coefficients RY page, together with the results for three to five qubits. The noise types fall into three regimes with qualitatively different effects on the spectrum:

  • Decoherent gate errors (BF, PF, DP) contract coefficient magnitudes. The absolute coefficient mean decays approximately exponentially with the noise level, with rates that vary across frequencies and ansätze, so the shape of the sampled magnitude spectrum can change. For coefficients whose relative standard deviation remains approximately constant, the absolute variance contracts approximately with \(\mu_c(\boldsymbol{\omega})^2\).
  • SPAM and damping errors (SP, ME, AD, PD) leave the measured spectrum largely intact. As they act only once per qubit at the circuit boundary, their effect on the coefficient magnitudes is small. Terminal PD preserves the \(Z\) expectation values exactly, ME multiplies all coefficients by \(1 - 2p\), and AD multiplies the nonzero-frequency coefficients by \(1 - p\) while shifting the constant term to \((1-p)c_{\boldsymbol{0}} + p\), i.e. towards positive values, as shown below.
  • Coherent gate errors (CGE) preserve the encoding-allowed frequencies. For a fixed realisation of the additive offsets, the frequency set is unchanged, and the sampled \(\mu_c(\boldsymbol{\omega})\) and \(\sigma_c(\boldsymbol{\omega})\) coincide with their noiseless values at every tested level for all ansätze. Exact absorption into the trainable angles is established for the SEA, HEA and RYA with \(R_Y\) encoding, while the unchanged statistics for the CRA are an empirical observation under the tested sampling protocol.

Our Figure 5 in the paper:

Real coefficient for \(\boldsymbol{\omega} = \boldsymbol{0}\) in a noiseless setting and under 3% Amplitude Damping (AD) for circuits with six qubits and \(R_Y\) encoding.

docs.title: Summary across Encodings and Qubit Counts
docs.text:
Our Figure 14 in the paper (Appendix "Quantitative Coefficient Results") summarises the coefficient mean \(\mu_c(\boldsymbol{\omega})\) for 1D (\(R_X\) and \(R_Y\) encoding) and 2D (\(R_X R_Y\) encoding) inputs and all qubit counts, only depicting the zero and maximum frequency-coefficient under DP, AD and CGE as representatives of the three noise regimes:

Absolute coefficient mean \(\mu_c(\boldsymbol{\omega})\) for the lowest frequency \(\boldsymbol{\omega}=\boldsymbol{0}\) and highest frequency \(\boldsymbol{\omega} = \boldsymbol{\omega}_\text{max}\) in the respective spectrum under the influence of varying noise levels. We considered the one-dimensional encodings \(R_X\) and \(R_Y\) (\(D\) = 1), and a two-dimensional encoding \(R_X R_Y\) (\(D\) = 2). The y-axes for each facet row are equal throughout the respective \(\boldsymbol{\omega}\), but differ in between.

The corresponding relative standard deviation is (Our Figure 15 in the paper)

Relative standard deviation \(\sigma_c(\boldsymbol{\omega})\) for the absolute coefficient mean values from Fig. 14.

DP causes an exponential decline of \(\mu_c(\boldsymbol{\omega})\) for both coefficient classes, all qubit counts, encodings and ansätze, which is steeper for larger qubit counts and the two-dimensional encoding, while \(\sigma_c(\boldsymbol{\omega})\) remains approximately constant. AD increases \(\mu_c(\boldsymbol{0})\) and decreases \(\sigma_c(\boldsymbol{0})\) following the affine shift of the constant term, most evidently for the SEA, and has an imperceptible effect at \(\boldsymbol{\omega}_\text{max}\). Under CGE, both quantities coincide with their noiseless values.

The detailed mean, standard deviations and covariances for varying qubit counts and encodings can be found in the corresponding pages on coefficients RX, coefficients RY and 2D-coefficients.

docs.title: Entanglement
docs.text: We quantify the entangling capability with the mean negativity \(\overline{\mathcal{N}}(\rho) = \frac{2}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \mathcal{N}_k(\rho) \in [0, 1]\), where \(\mathcal{N}_k(\rho)\) is the negativity of the bipartition of qubit \(k\) versus the remaining qubits, i.e. the absolute sum of the negative eigenvalues of the partial transpose \(\rho^{T_k}\). In contrast to the Meyer-Wallach measure, the negativity is defined for pure and mixed states alike, such that the noiseless and the noisy experiments use the same measure. The entangling capability is the average of \(\overline{\mathcal{N}}\) over randomly sampled parameters, evaluated on the density matrix at \(\boldsymbol{x} = \boldsymbol{0}\). Note that the mean negativity only captures the average entanglement between single qubits and the rest of the system, such that ansätze with a similar value may still generate structurally different entangled states. The abbreviations of the ansätze and noise types are explained on the Setup page.

docs.title: Noiseless Circuits
docs.text:
Our Figure 8 in the paper:

Entangling capability, measured by the mean negativity \(\overline{\mathcal{N}}\) averaged over randomly sampled parameters, for the considered ansätze in a noiseless environment. The bars represent the mean values with error bars from the minimum to maximum highlighted in red across the five seeds.

An increasing qubit count leads to a higher overall value for the entangling capability, while the specific values for the SEA, HEA and RYA are similar. The CRA, which uses controlled rotations as entangling gates, has a lower entangling capability for more than four qubits.

docs.title: Under the Influence of Noise
docs.text:
Our Figure 9 in the paper:

Entangling capability, measured by the mean negativity \(\overline{\mathcal{N}}\) averaged over randomly sampled parameters, under the influence of increasing noise levels. Points represent the mean of five seeds and lines are a linear interpolation to guide the eye. The zero-noise points correspond to the values in Fig. 8. As the relative standard deviation across the five seeds is small (below 1.8%), the mean entangling capability is representative.

The three noise regimes identified for the coefficients are reflected in the entangling capability as well: Decoherent gate errors (BF, PF and DP) reduce the entangling capability substantially for all ansätze and qubit counts, and the decrease appears to be exponential in the noise level, mirroring the exponential contraction of the Fourier coefficients. SPAM and damping errors (SP, ME, AD and PD), which act only once per qubit at the boundary of the circuit, lead to a slight decrease of the entangling capability over the tested noise levels. The sampled mean negativity under coherent gate errors (CGE) remains close to its noiseless value.

docs.title: Expressibility
docs.text: Expressibility is quantified by the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence of the fidelity distribution of randomly sampled states (evaluated at \(\boldsymbol{x} = \boldsymbol{0}\)) from the Haar reference distribution, where lower values indicate higher expressibility. For mixed states, the squared Uhlmann fidelity is used while the pure-state Haar reference is retained, so changes in the divergence can reflect changes in state exploration as well as mixedness. The least expressive case, i.e. the empty circuit, yields the upper bound \((2^n - 1)\ln(n_\text{bins})\) with \(n_\text{bins} = 75 n\) equal-width fidelity bins for \(n\) qubits. The abbreviations of the ansätze and noise types are explained on the Setup page.

docs.title: Expressibility under Noise
docs.text:
Our Figure 7 in the paper:

KL divergence of the fidelity distribution from the Haar reference under increasing noise levels, with lower values indicating higher expressibility. Points represent the mean over the five seeds. The dotted lines mark the upper bound \((2^n-1)\ln(75n)\) for each qubit count and hence the least expressive case.

Only the mean over the five seeds is shown, as the relative standard deviation across seeds is below 5% on average and reaches at most 29%, the latter only for coherent gate errors.

  • Without noise, the ranking follows the ansatz structure. The SEA is the most expressive ansatz for four or more qubits, followed by the HEA and CRA, while the RYA shows the largest KL divergence, as it generates only states with real amplitudes at zero input.
  • Decoherent gate errors equalise the expressibility. BF, PF and DP increase the KL divergence by up to three orders of magnitude already at 0.5%, and at 3% all ansätze lie within about one order of magnitude of the respective upper bound. The noiseless ranking of the SEA and the CRA is reversed, consistent with the number of noisy gates per layer, but noise level and qubit count dominate the KL divergence.
  • SPAM and damping errors have a small effect. At 3%, they increase the KL divergence to values of order one for SPAM errors and of order 0.1 to 0.5 for damping errors, one to two orders of magnitude below those for decoherent gate errors. For the RYA, small levels of SP, ME and PD even reduce the KL divergence slightly, as the measure does not distinguish between a Haar-like distribution generated by the ansatz and one caused by mixing.
  • Coherent gate errors have little effect on the sampled expressibility. The CGE curves remain close to their noiseless values over the tested levels.

docs.title: Expressibility of Deeper Circuits
docs.text:
Our Figure 16 in the paper (Appendix "Expressibility of Deeper Circuits"):

KL divergence of the fidelity distribution from the Haar reference for \(L \in \{1, 2, 4\}\) encoding layers at a fixed noise level of 3% for each noise type; lower values indicate higher expressibility. The first column shows the noiseless reference. Points represent the mean over the five seeds. The dotted lines mark the upper bound for the KL divergence at a certain qubit count and hence the least expressive case. The values for \(L = 1\) correspond to the 3% points in Fig. 7.

Without noise and under coherent gate errors, the KL divergence of the SEA does not change with depth, whereas the HEA and the CRA decrease by about one order of magnitude from one to two layers for four and more qubits and then level off at the values of the SEA. The RYA remains at its single-layer value of about 0.2 for all depths, as additional real-valued gates do not lift the restriction to real amplitudes. Under decoherent gate errors, the KL divergence increases monotonically with depth for all ansätze and qubit counts and approaches the upper bound, while SPAM and damping errors act only once per qubit at the circuit boundary and are therefore independent of depth.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text: Our implementation heavily relies on our QML Essentials package. Furthermore we use Kedro to manage our experiments.

docs.title: Noise Models
docs.text:
The noise model we use in our experiments can be summarized as follows:

Here, \(\mathcal{N}_{SP}\) describes state preparation noise, \(\mathcal{N}_{G}\) gate noise and \(\mathcal{N}_{D}\) circuit noise. Coherent gate errors are modelled by \(\epsilon\).

The gate noise \(\mathcal{N}_G\) can be decomposed as follows:

At the end of the circuit the noise model \(\mathcal{N}_D\) is applied:

The noise types fall into four groups, which differ in where and how often a channel acts during one circuit evaluation (Table 1 in the paper):

Group Noise types Placement Applications Decoherent gate errors Bit Flip (BF), Phase Flip (PF), Depolarizing (DP) after every gate \(N_g\) (number of local gate-noise insertions) Damping errors Amplitude Damping (AD), Phase Damping (PD) once per qubit at the end of the circuit \(n\) State preparation and measurement (SPAM) errors State Preparation (SP), Measurement (ME) once per qubit at the beginning / end of the circuit \(n\) Coherent gate errors (CGE) additive rotation-angle offsets \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, p_\text{cge}^2)\) every parametrised rotation \(N_r\) (number of rotation angles)

Channel probabilities \(p\) are specified per application, whereas \(p_\text{cge}\) is the standard deviation of the additive angle error in radians. Gate noise acts separately on each wire of a gate, so equal local probabilities do not imply equal accumulated noise across ansätze. For the coefficient and training experiments, one realisation of the coherent offsets per circuit layout is kept fixed across inputs, parameter samples, optimisation steps and seeds, and the same standardised offsets are scaled with \(p_\text{cge}\) across noise levels. The expressibility and entanglement experiments instead sample the coherent offsets across the state batch.

docs.title: Ansaetze
docs.text: We use the following ansaetze throughout our experiments (Figure 10 in the paper, shown for four qubits). In the plots, the ansätze are abbreviated as SEA, HEA, RYA and CRA. The RYA and CRA are inspired by circuits 15 and 19 of Sim et al. (2019) and are called Circuit_20 and Circuit_19 in the code and in the result data, respectively.

docs.title: Experimental Protocol
docs.text:
Unless stated otherwise, experiments use a single encoding layer (\(L = 1\)), \(n \in [3\dots 6]\) qubits and the mean of the local \(Z\) expectation values as readout. The deeper-circuit expressibility study additionally tests \(L = 2\) and \(L = 4\) at a fixed noise level of 3% and without noise. The main noise sweeps use seven linearly increasing levels from 0% to 3% in steps of 0.5%. Trainable parameters are sampled uniformly from \([0, 2\pi]\) with five seeds for the one-dimensional coefficient, expressibility and entanglement experiments, two for the two-dimensional coefficient experiments and ten for the training experiments.

  • Coefficients: one-dimensional (\(R_X\), \(R_Y\) or \(R_Z\) encoding, \(D = 1\)) and two-dimensional (\(R_X R_Y\) encoding, \(D = 2\)) inputs; \(250 \times 2^n\) parameter vectors per seed for \(D = 1\) and 250 per seed for \(D = 2\). The two-dimensional experiments use two seeds.
  • Expressibility and entanglement are evaluated on the density matrix at \(\boldsymbol{x} = \boldsymbol{0}\), as these descriptors only depend on the trainable layers. Entanglement uses \(250 \times 2^n\) parameter vectors per seed, while expressibility uses two independent batches of that size to form \(250 \times 2^n\) state pairs and \(75 n\) equal-width fidelity bins.
  • Training uses six-qubit circuits with \(R_Y\) encoding on ten randomly generated Fourier series with the same frequency set as the model and a maximum absolute target value of \(a = 0.5\), using Adam (learning rate 0.01) for 1000 steps. The loss is the squared complex coefficient error summed over all frequencies, which equals the mean squared error (MSE) on an exact-period grid and approximates it on the configured training grid (see Training). Noisy training uses a noise level of 3% for each noise type.

docs.title: Training
docs.text: We train six-qubit QFMs with \(R_Y\) encoding on randomly generated Fourier series (see Setup) by minimising the squared complex coefficient error summed over all frequencies with Adam (learning rate 0.01) for 1000 steps. During training we record the mean squared error (MSE), the learned absolute coefficients \(\lvert c_{\boldsymbol{\omega}} \rvert\), the squared coefficient error \(\Delta c_{\boldsymbol{\omega}} = \lvert c_{\boldsymbol{\omega}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) - c'_{\boldsymbol{\omega}} \rvert^2\) between the learned and the target coefficients and the entangling capability. On an evenly spaced grid covering exactly one period without aliasing or a repeated endpoint, Parseval's identity relates the two error metrics via \(\text{MSE} = \sum_{\boldsymbol{\omega}} \Delta c_{\boldsymbol{\omega}}\). The configured training grid uses 38 points on \([-3.1415, 3.1415)\), so this equality holds only approximately for the recorded MSE. Noisy training uses a noise level of 3% for each noise type. The abbreviations of the ansätze and noise types are explained on the Setup page.

docs.title: Noiseless Training
docs.text:
Our Figure 3 in the paper:

Training performance in a noiseless setting for a single randomly generated problem instance (seed 1000) during training of 1000 steps. Lines represent the mean, and shaded areas show the standard deviation over ten parameter initialisation seeds. Left: The MSE during training. Right: The learned absolute coefficients of the QFMs. The coefficients of the objective Fourier series are marked with dashed lines.

For this problem instance, the HEA and CRA retain larger errors, while the RYA and the SEA achieve lower MSEs, with the SEA performing best. Across all ansätze, most of the learned coefficients that correspond to lower frequencies converge to the targets, whereas the ansätze that converge to a higher MSE especially fail to match higher-frequency coefficients. Frequency availability alone therefore does not guarantee a match to the target coefficients within the fixed optimisation budget, even without noise.

docs.title: Final Training Performance under Noise
docs.text:
Our Figure 6 in the paper:

Training performance after 1000 training steps in the noiseless setting and under each noise type (3%), averaged over ten model parameter initialisation seeds and ten randomly generated problem instances. Bars represent the mean and error bars the standard deviation over the 10 × 10 configurations. Left: final MSE for each ansatz (rows) and noise type. Right: final squared coefficient error \(\Delta c_{\boldsymbol{\omega}}\) between the learned coefficients \(c_{\boldsymbol{\omega}}(\boldsymbol{\theta})\) and the target coefficients \(c'_{\boldsymbol{\omega}}\) for each frequency \(\boldsymbol{\omega}\).

Decoherent gate errors raise the MSE to a similar level of approximately 0.02 for all ansätze, with DP typically being the most harmful, whereas SPAM and damping errors leave the MSE at its noiseless level. Consequently, the SEA, which achieves the lowest noiseless fitting errors, loses much of this advantage under decoherent gate errors. For fixed coherent gate errors, the final MSE and the coefficient errors coincide with the noiseless values for every ansatz, as the fixed offsets are compensated during training. Decoherent gate errors increase \(\Delta c_{\boldsymbol{\omega}}\) predominantly for the higher frequencies, in line with the contraction of the coefficients observed on the Coefficients page: the optimiser counteracts the contraction for the low-frequency coefficients but leaves larger residuals at high frequencies. The frequencies with numerically vanishing absolute coefficient means in the noiseless HEA retain a constant error regardless of the noise type, and the higher-frequency coefficients of the RYA and the CRA are not matched even without noise.

docs.title: Mean Squared Error
docs.text:
Our Figure 17 in the paper (Appendix "Training Curves"):

The MSE over ten parameter initialisation seeds and ten randomly generated problem instances during training in the noiseless setting and under each noise type (3%). Lines represent the mean, and shaded areas show the standard deviation over the 10 × 10 configurations.

docs.title: Squared Coefficient Error
docs.text:
Our Figure 18 in the paper:

The squared coefficient error \(\Delta c_{\boldsymbol{\omega}}\) averaged over ten model parameter initialisation seeds and ten randomly generated problem instances during training in the noiseless setting and under each noise type (3%). Lines represent the mean, and shaded areas show the standard deviation over the 10 × 10 configurations.

All configurations reach a plateau before the end of the training, such that the final values in Fig. 6 reflect the fitting error achieved under the chosen optimiser and training budget. Lower frequencies are matched within the first few hundred steps, whereas higher frequencies converge more slowly.

docs.title: Coefficients during Training for Problem Instances
docs.text:
In the following, we show the learned absolute coefficients of the QFMs averaged over ten parameter model initialisation seeds for each single randomly generated problem instance with seeds \([1000\dots 1009]\) and different types of noise (3%) during training of 1000 steps. In the figures the shaded areas correspond to the standard deviation across the parameter initialisation seeds from the mean. The coefficients of the objective Fourier series are marked with dashed lines. Under decoherent gate errors, the low-frequency coefficients still converge to their targets, whereas the high-frequency coefficients saturate below their targets, such that the learned spectrum is tilted towards the low frequencies relative to the target. Since the coherent gate errors are quasi-static, the offsets remain fixed across training steps and the curves are indistinguishable from the noiseless ones.

docs.title: Entanglement during Training
docs.text:
Our Figure 20 in the paper (Appendix "Entanglement during Training"):

Entangling capability, measured by the mean negativity \(\overline{\mathcal{N}}\) (see Entanglement) during training. Lines represent the mean over ten parameter initialisation seeds and ten problem generation seeds. Shaded areas represent the standard deviation.

The orders of magnitude of the entangling capability under the different noise types are similar to those measured for randomly sampled parameters. Over the course of the training we observe a decrease in the entangling capability for most configurations (with the exception of damping errors), which is more pronounced in some experiments (e.g. SEA with DP) but consistent across all tested problem and model initialisation seeds for each configuration. The similar mean negativities of the SEA, HEA and RYA accompany different MSEs, so this zero-input descriptor alone does not determine fitting performance on the tested tasks.
